To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the majority of liver recipients who have been immunosuppression‐free for > 8 years have normal graft and patient outcomes; (2) liver histology remains essential to assess allograph health; and (3) the development of noninvasive but reliable biomarkers is urgently needed.

(i) liver histology remains an essential tool to assess allograph health and guide immunotherapy management; (ii) immunosuppression should be withdrawn in selected, stable liver transplant recipients; (iii) the majority of patients who are eligible for withdrawal will be operationally tolerant; (iv) histologic assessment of allograft health should be performed in patients who are eligible to undergo immunosuppression trials; and (v) histologic assessment should continue after immunosuppression cessation

(i) liver histology remains a critical tool in the management of the long‐term liver transplant recipient, (ii) the histologic assessment of liver transplant biopsies requires an understanding of the histologic changes associated with chronic rejection, and (iii) the histologic changes of chronic rejection can be subtle and easily misinterpreted, especially in the presence of concomitant fibrosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new biomarkers for the diagnosis of rejection and tolerance after liver transplantation.
the immunological mechanisms that lead to the establishment of long‐term tolerance to a transplanted organ, and with the identification of biomarkers of tolerance.

the following: (a) the mechanisms of immune tolerance after liver transplantation (b) biomarkers to identify patients at risk of immunological injury and/or rejection, (c) the role of the microbiome in the development of tolerance and (d) the development and testing of novel immunomodulators for use in liver transplant recipients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the field is at a crossroads.

the field of immunosuppressant withdrawal has made great strides in identifying the optimal patient for withdrawal, and that this patient population has a high rate of tolerance, but that the histologic and clinical implications of immunologic quiescence in this population remain unclear.
immunosuppression should be minimized in highly selected recipients and that liver histology remains essential to guide immunosuppressive management.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immunosuppression‐withdrawal trials are a success.
immunosuppression should be minimized, not maximized.
immunosuppression in liver transplant recipients can be completely and safely withdrawn from highly selected subsets of adult and pediatric recipients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver biopsy is a valuable tool in the management of liver transplant recipients, and it is a tool that is underutilized.
the liver biopsy remains a critical tool to guide immunosuppressive management.
the immunological and histological assessment of the allograft is the best tool we have to guide immunosuppressive management.
